items.title: Unpaid TV licence or cycling on pavement could bar people from settling in UK
items.summary:
Exclusive: New immigration rules will introduce strict threshold where any adult conviction triggers mandatory refusal

People could be barred from settling in the UK over minor infractions such as cycling on the pavement or failing to pay a TV licence, ministers have been warned before the introduction of new “earned settlement” rules.

Under the plans, which are to come into effect next year, securing indefinite leave to remain will become significantly harder for many people. The rules introduce a strict new threshold where any adult conviction resulting in a court disposal – including fines, community orders, conditional cautions, and absolute or conditional discharges – triggers mandatory refusal.

items.t: Unpaid TV licence or cycling on pavement could bar people from settling in UK

items.title: Abusers are not ‘other’ – they are all around us | Letters
items.summary:
Male sexual violence against women is fuelled by misogyny, writes Sarah Mulholland

The courage of Joanne Young is powerful, and it could be pivotal (Joanne Young praised for bravery in exposing rape by husband and strangers, 20 November). The publicity given to high-profile cases such as those of Russell Brand, Jeffrey Epstein and Mohamed Al Fayed is understandable, but it runs the risk of serving as a convenient deflector, allowing us to comfort ourselves that rapists and sexual abusers are somehow “other”.

Indeed, one of the most pernicious rape myths is the belief that rape is perpetrated by men of a different social or economic status, of a different ethnicity or culture – outsiders from whom we can distance ourselves.

items.t: Abusers are not ‘other’ – they are all around us | Letters

items.title: Court to determine if Alaska’s seizure of pilot’s plane for carrying beer violates the Eighth Amendment
items.summary:
The Supreme Court will hear oral argument on Tuesday in an Alaskan bush pilot’s challenge to the forfeiture of his $95,000 airplane. Prosecutors sought that forfeiture on the theory that the pilot, Ken Jouppi, must have known a passenger was bringing beer to an Alaskan village where alcohol is prohibited. That penalty, Jouppi argues, violates the Eighth Amendment’s ban on excessive fines.

The case before the court began in April 2012, when Jouppi, who is now 83 years old, was scheduled to fly a passenger from Fairbanks to Beaver, Alaska – less than a one-hour flight. Beaver, whose population was reported as 48 in the 2020 census, is a “dry” village: it bars not only the sale of alcohol, but also the importation and possession of alcohol. There are no roads to or from the village, and the closest hospital is in Fairbanks.

Before Jouppi took off for Beaver, state troopers arrived at the airport with a warrant to search his plane. According to the state , law enforcement officials had “receiv[ed] information that Jouppi had repeatedly transported passengers with alcohol to” dry villages. They found the equivalent of three cases of beer that his passenger was bringing to her husband, who works in Beaver, and charged both the passenger and Jouppi (as well as his company) with knowingly bringing alcohol to a “dry” village.

The passenger pleaded guilty. Jouppi went to trial, where he was found guilty. The trial judge sentenced him to three days in prison and ordered him to pay a fine of $1,500.

Under state law, prosecutors also sought to forfeit Jouppi’s plane. The Alaska…
items.t: Court to determine if Alaska’s seizure of pilot’s plane for carrying beer violates the Eighth Amendment

items.title: ‘She was so not regretful about killing her husband’: the Iranian film that shines a light on blood money and retributive justice
items.summary:
The co-director of An Eye for an Eye, Tanaz Eshaghian, reveals how she came to make a documentary about a woman facing the threat of execution from her husband’s family – as sanctioned by sharia law

“Even though I was raised here,” says the Iranian-American film-maker Tanaz Eshaghian from her home in New York, “I was brought up with the understanding that there are things that you do and things that you don’t do.” Take her 2006 autobiographical feature, Love Iranian-American Style, about her experience of dating in her 20s, which was, she says, “about how I was supposed to marry a nice Iranian man and stay a virgin”. But by the time she’d graduated from Brown University in Rhode Island “that ship had sailed”, she laughs.

Since Love Iranian-American Style, she has made equally taboo-breaking documentaries about a women’s prison in Afghanistan (Love Crimes of Kabul, 2011), trans people in Iran (Be Like Others, 2008) and disabled teenagers in Pakistan (As Far As They Can Run, 2022). And with each new project, the duality of her heritage (Eshaghian emigrated to the US not long after the Iranian revolution when she was six) has spurred her to focus eastwards, closer to where she was born. “When you’ve been raised in the west you can see how similar the thinking is,” Eshaghian says of the similarities she’s found there: “the conservative thinking, the place of women, what’s allowed, what’s important”.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘She was so not regretful about killing her husband’: the Iranian film that shines a light on blood money and retributive justice

Ministers will create a new stalking offence so that victims will no longer have to prove fear or distress to seek protection under the law, the Home Office has announced.

Under current laws, the underlying offence of harassment in England and Wales, as well as additional factors such as the victim’s alarm, must be established for it to be considered stalking. The new law, alongside other changes, will focus on the perpetrator’s behaviour instead, officials said.

items.summary:
The holiday shopping season is approaching, and unfortunately, increases in the cost of living due to inflation have made it harder for households to purchase holiday presents without exceeding their budgets. As a result, consumers are scrutinizing the prices they pay, including the sales taxes added to their purchases. One increasingly relevant question is whether it makes economic sense for Los Angeles residents to travel to neighboring cities to take advantage of lower sales tax rates.

Recently, Los Angeles voters approved Measure FD, which would increase the city’s sales tax rate by another 0.5 percentage points to help fund the Los Angeles Fire Department. This will increase the combined sales tax rate in Los Angeles is 10.75%. This rate is similar to other cities in the Los Angeles metropolitan area and has rates as high as 11.50%.

Compare this to neighboring Orange County, where some cities have considerably lower sales tax rates of 7.75%. This discrepancy is because these cities have little or no local sales taxes.

In the past, the sales tax rates for Los Angeles County and Orange County were almost equal. In 1990, the combined sales tax rate in Los Angeles was approximately 6.75% while most cities in Orange County were 6.25% .

A person who lives in Los Angeles might consider driving to Orange County and shopping where the sales tax rate is substantially lower. This is typically a tactic people done by people living close to a state with low or no sales taxes.

items.title: Build Your Own Book, Own Your Own Career
items.summary:
Getty Images 

In a recent conversation with John Cashman , President of Major, Lindsey & Africa, I explored what it really takes for lawyers to own their careers, from the decision to move firms to the book of business that makes a move possible. 

In his appearance on the “Be That Lawyer” podcast, John brought the vantage point of someone who leads a top legal search firm and has seen thousands of lateral moves up close. 

His message was candid: Great legal work matters, but a lawyer’s career is shaped just as much by client relationships, clear-eyed decisions, and an understanding of the business of law. 

More Than Money 

John’s answer about his “biggest mistake” was one every lawyer considering a move should hear. 

As a young lawyer, he accepted an offer to join Winston & Strawn. His firm sweetened the pot with a counteroffer, and he stayed. 

A year later, he was at Winston & Strawn anyway. 

The ‘Cloudiness’ Problem 

Law firms need to learn business leadership and operations if they want to attract the candidates they’re after. 

Too often, the message to a recruit is that compensation will get figured out later, with no clear path laid out.

The ’95-5′ Differentiator — With Some Exceptions 

While it’s much easier for a lawyer to move if they have a book of business, there are some exceptions. 

And it isn’t only about the revenue.

items.t: Build Your Own Book, Own Your Own Career

items.title: Which Is It: Do We Need To ‘Protect Our Geniuses’ Or Keep China From Outpacing Us On AI At All Costs?
items.summary:
Jensen Huang had extramarital affairs with multiple women. Two are reportedly subordinates at Nvidia. Another was a Chinese national who was in touch with an official at China’s top spy agency during the affair.

Nvidia builds the infrastructure that the AI boom depends on. It makes the best computer chips in the world.

Some of these chips are important. We don’t want them falling into the hands of our authoritarian rival on the world stage, China.

Yet, under Huang’s leadership, Nvidia’s restricted hardware indeed made its way to China. While it’s not entirely evident yet exactly how Huang’s Chinese mistress fits into the story, it is a fact that banned and restricted Nvidia chips were illegally shipped to China. Among the end buyers was the Chinese military.

None of this mattered to Donald Trump. The White House is now little more than a protection racket. With Huang in charge, Nvidia donated millions to Trump’s inauguration fund and ballroom , thereby securing Trump’s future patronage.

Moreover, Trump owns tens of thousands of shares of Nvidia stock. When Huang was briefly ousted, the value of that stock plummeted. After Trump leaned on Nvidia’s board over the weekend to get it to reinstate Huang, Nvidia shares soared Monday. Trump recovered millions.

“We have to protect our geniuses, and he’s clearly a genius,” said Trump of Huang as he, Trump, bragged about his intervention in getting Nvidia’s board to reverse its decision. Trump also self-servingly imagined that Huang might have taken a job in China had Nvidia’s CEO position not remained his.

items.title: Skadden Does NOT Announce Raises, But Did Remind Associates To Be Thankful For Firm’s AI Investments!
items.summary:
Under normal circumstances, it’s nice to get a Thanksgiving message from firm leadership. Sure, they’re making you work the holiday turning documents on a deal that the partners already know will fall through, but it’s the thought that counts.

But with every firm blasting out mass emails announcing (long overdue) raises and annual bonuses, and heightened special bonuses, any email from the managing partner that pops up in an associate’s inbox carries certain… expectations. And if the firm isn’t ready to tell everyone about raises, it’s best to keep quiet.

By way of context, the last time Cravath announced big compensation news, Skadden matched within a day . So when the firm received a mass email from Jeremy London titled “A Note of Thanks.” Associates opened it planning to see the now-familiar salary chart. What they got was this:

As we head into Thanksgiving, I have been thinking about the past two years, a time of real evolution for Skadden and our profession, and about how far we have come together.

…

Periods of change test an institution’s values and culture. They ask us to hold on to what makes us distinctive even as so much around us evolves, and they take deliberate effort to keep our community at the center of where we are headed. We have met that test while laying the groundwork for what comes next, and that work is now paying off.

Not the ideal start, but attorneys probably assumed this was just a little preamble. Like that cooking blog they checked in advance of Thanksgiving that waxed philosophic about their favorite Butternut Squash memories before…
items.t: Skadden Does NOT Announce Raises, But Did Remind Associates To Be Thankful For Firm’s AI Investments!

items.title: White House Looks Ready To Give Up On Its Controversial Federal Judge Pick
items.summary:
Donald Trump does not usually take no for an answer from Republican senators. That goes double for John Cornyn, who is leaving the Senate after nearly 24 years because Trump backed Ken Paxton against him in the primary. (Paxton then lost to Democrat James Talarico anyway.) But on T. Elliot Gaiser , it looks like the White House may be ready to concede at least one point.

According to Reuters, the White House has started an FBI background check on Steve Fahey, the former federal prosecutor Cornyn has been pushing for months for a seat on the federal bench in Dallas. That suggests the administration is thinking about nominating Fahey instead of Gaiser. It’s a notable course change for a White House that is racing to cram as many lifetime appointments as possible through the lame-duck Senate before Democrats take control on January 3. It’s also a change of tune. Last week, Senator Ted Cruz said the White House had told him a new nominee would be “impossible” to confirm because the FBI’s background check would take too long. His full statement:

If the Senate Judiciary Committee does not move Gaiser forward, the people of Texas will pay the price because it will effectively give the judicial seat to the Democrats, who will keep it vacant in perpetuity.

Turns out the FBI can run a background check after all.

Trump picked Gaiser, currently the Assistant Attorney General for the Office of Legal Counsel, for the Northern District of Texas seat Judge Jane Boyle left when she took senior status. Cornyn refused to return his blue slip , so under the Judiciary Committee’s current…
items.t: White House Looks Ready To Give Up On Its Controversial Federal Judge Pick

items.title: Court to hear argument on whether school employees may bring suit under Title IX
items.summary:
The federal law known as Title IX prohibits sex-based discrimination by schools that receive federal funding. On November 30, the Supreme Court will hear oral argument in a dispute over whether the law allows school employees to bring lawsuits alleging sex discrimination, or whether such employees must instead rely on a different federal law, Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, that specifically provides a remedy for sex-based employment discrimination but also imposes constraints not found in Title IX. The employees seeking to bring the lawsuits under Title IX will face a bench that has become increasingly reluctant to permit private plaintiffs to bring lawsuits unless the federal statute at issue clearly authorizes them.

The plaintiffs in the case are two former employees of Georgia’s state university system. Thomas Crowther worked as an art professor at Augusta University. When he was accused of inappropriate conduct by several students, including sexual harassment, the university initially suspended him for one semester and then declined to renew his contract, prompting Crowther to file a lawsuit against the university for sex discrimination and retaliation.

Machelle Joseph was the head women’s basketball coach at Georgia Tech. She was fired in 2019 after an investigation raised concerns about mistreatment of players. Before her termination, Joseph had repeatedly complained about her team receiving fewer resources than the men’s team. Joseph filed a lawsuit against the university for sex discrimination and retaliation.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th…

items.title: Trying To Move Thanksgiving Has Not Gone Well, Historically Speaking
items.summary:
Ed. Note: Welcome to our daily feature Trivia Question of the Day! 

Thanksgiving’s date is set by federal law as the fourth Thursday in November — but that law exists only because a president once tried to move the holiday himself. In 1939, at the urging of retailers who wanted a longer Christmas shopping season, he proclaimed Thanksgiving a week early. States revolted, the calendar descended into chaos, and the rescheduled holiday picked up what mocking nickname? 

Hint: The president was Franklin D. Roosevelt, who did it three years running. The country split — nearly half the states kept the traditional date, and a few observed both — until Congress ended the mess by fixing Thanksgiving in law, choosing the fourth Thursday over the last. 

See the answer on the next page.

items.title: 3 More Questions For A Patent Litigator Turned Legal Recruiter (Part II)

(Image via Getty) 

Last time, I presented Part 1 of my written interview with a former patent litigator turned legal recruiter, Khurram Naik. That column presented his answer to the first of my three questions and focused on the lessons shared by his podcast guests that have relevance to his lateral candidates. What follows are Khurram’s answers to my remaining two questions. As usual, I have added some brief commentary to his answers below, but have otherwise presented his answers as he provided them.

Gaston Kroub: What’s the role of a legal podcast like yours? 

Khurram Naik: Legal media focus on outcomes, like what a court decided in a particular matter. But there’s little insight into the process that led to those outcomes. Lawyers make concerted decisions over a period of time and develop the judgement to direct those outcomes. That’s what the podcast uncovers. 

There is the problem of the vanilla middle. So many interviews with lawyers have rehearsed answers to softball questions. What I’ve found much more interesting are the bookends to the vanilla middle: 1) what are the real challenges and setbacks exceptional lawyers face, and 2) what are the smart calls they’ve made. 

The first inquiry humanizes skilled lawyers so we can actually learn from them. The second inquiry sidesteps the “I’m humbled to announce, it was a team effort, etc.” reaction to discussing successes so we can actually learn what someone did that was skillful.

items.title: 5 Habits That Keep Great Legal Rainmakers On Top Of Their Game
items.summary:
I’ve been watching tennis for more than 45 years, from Jimmy Connors to Roger Federer and Rafael Nadal, and I still find myself watching Carlos Alcaraz and wondering how he got to a ball I was sure was past him. Then he’ll hit a drop shot from the baseline so soft it barely gets over the net, and I’ll wonder how he even thought to try it. I’ll leave the greatest-of-all-time debate to somebody else, but this guy still shows me things I don’t remember seeing anyone else do. 

There’s no arguing with his natural talent, but what fascinates me is what it takes to get to that level and keep finding ways to get better when everyone else is trying to catch you. I see a version of that in the lawyers I work with. After helping hundreds of attorneys build their books of business, I can tell you that the ones who stay at the top don’t all have the same personality. Some would happily work a room of 200 people, while others would rather spend an hour with one person they genuinely want to know. What they do have in common are five habits that keep working long after their first big year. 

1. Make Business Development A Non-negotiable 

Most lawyers I know say business development is important, but would you know it from looking at their calendars? If the call to a referral partner is the first thing you bump when a client matter heats up, and you never reschedule it, you’ve already decided where business development ranks. The best rainmakers take their commitments to future clients as seriously as they take the work they’re doing for current ones. An urgent matter may force you to…
items.t: 5 Habits That Keep Great Legal Rainmakers On Top Of Their Game

items.title: The People Who Got You Home For Thanksgiving
items.summary:
One Christmas in Chicago, when I was 10 or 11, I got a toolbox. A set of wooden levers held each tool in place. I could turn one, lift out a saw, and get to work, assuming my parents had meant to give a 10-year-old a saw. I chose to assume they had. I just needed something to cut.

The lumberyard a few blocks from our house seemed like the place to start. I walked over with my toolbox and some change and asked the manager if I could buy a few scraps. He asked to see my tools. Now, if you’ve ever given a kid a toolbox, you know the next best present is a chance to open it and show you what’s inside.

That man filled a paper bag with pieces of wood and threw in screws and nails. When I asked what I owed him, he told me to take it. You’d think I could tell you what I built with all that wood. I can’t. But more than 40 years later, I can still see those little levers, and I remember the man who took the time to watch me turn them.

Thanksgiving brings people like him to mind. After nearly 30 years as a lawyer, I could fill a legal pad with the names of people who gave me something I needed at just the right moment. Some would have to think for a minute to remember what they did. That strikes me as a good reason to tell them. For most of us, the list starts pretty close to home.

The last deposition before dinner 

Consider what it takes to get a lawyer home for Thanksgiving. You have a deposition on Wednesday morning. You tell your family you’ll be on the road by lunch, using the same math that lets you tell a judge, “I have just a few more questions.” This time you make it.…

items.title: ‘The Best Justice System In The World’ Has A Jury Problem
items.summary:
Courtroom dramas give us a reassuring picture of justice: a case goes to trial, a jury hears the evidence, and the right verdict arrives before the credits roll. Real life is considerably less tidy. In The Best Justice System in the World , Suja A. Thomas , a law professor at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, uses humor to examine how government and corporations can deprive ordinary people of their right to a jury trial. The film is meant to make viewers laugh, then think deeply about what happens when the joke is on someone facing the justice system.

Plea deals can pressure people to give up a jury trial, even when they may be innocent. In civil cases, summary judgment and arbitration can keep discrimination and harassment claims from reaching a jury, too. The film follows people caught in those systems and asks what happens when decisions with life-changing consequences are left to prosecutors, judges, or private arbitrators. Juries remain a familiar fixture on TV. In real life, they can be more of a special guest.

For Thomas, this is personal. The discrimination she and her family experienced helped inspire her to become a lawyer. She later grew concerned that jury trials were becoming increasingly rare. In her director’s statement, she calls juries “a last line of defense” against improper prosecution. That sounds less like legal theory than a warning. The film’s bluntest assessment is even shorter: “We’re f****d.”

Thomas spent decades as a lawyer and law professor trying to draw attention to these issues through articles, books, op-eds, and public…
items.t: ‘The Best Justice System In The World’ Has A Jury Problem

items.title: Refugees, asylum, and Supreme Court exceptionalism
items.summary:
American exceptionalism, the idea that the United States is uniquely virtuous, has deep roots that predate the nation itself. The founders of New England, in words echoed by President Ronald Reagan, famously declared that it was to be “as a citty upon a Hill. The eies of all people are upon us .”

At best, American exceptionalism can be beneficent in intent and beneficial in result. In time the New England states would become leaders in the abolition of slavery. Closer to our time, the United States would translate its victory in the Second Word War into the Marshall Plan, the World Bank, and the currently embattled international legal order under the aegis of the United Nations. The 18th Amendment , the juvenile death penalty (until 2005 ), and the failure to guarantee a right to healthcare furnish examples of exceptionalism gone wrong.

And then there is the Supreme Court’s wariness toward international law. At the Founding and for decades thereafter, the court tended to embrace “the law of nations,” either as a guide to interpreting relevant statutes or even as furnishing a rule of decision in appropriate circumstances. In more recent times, however, majorities have balked at viewing treaties as self-executing, taking guidance from the International Court of Justice, or applying statutes that expressly incorporate “the law of nations” into domestic law. 

A grant of certiorari just this month will likely confirm the trend. The case is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services , in which the justices will review one of the Trump…
items.t: Refugees, asylum, and Supreme Court exceptionalism

items.title: Which justices favor the Trump administration the most (and least) on the emergency docket?
items.summary:
When the Supreme Court rejected President Donald Trump’s attempt to remove Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook in June, the justices divided in a manner that would have been difficult to predict from some perceptions of the court. Chief Justice John Roberts and Justice Brett Kavanaugh joined Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan, and Ketanji Brown Jackson to leave Cook in office while the case proceeded. Justices Clarence Thomas, Samuel Alito, Neil Gorsuch, and Amy Coney Barrett dissented. The administration lost, but the court’s disagreement did not reflect the familiar ideological split.

Four months later, the administration lost another emergency application, this time in a dispute over medical care for transgender federal prisoners. In Trump v. Kingdom , Thomas and Alito indicated that they would have granted the requested stay, but no other justice publicly held that position. Unlike Trump v. Cook , which produced a signed opinion after oral argument, the Kingdom order disclosed nothing about the reasoning or votes behind the court’s denial.

The contrast points to a recurring theme of the Supreme Court’s emergency decisions: Although the conservative justices are often lumped together as “pro-Trump,” their rulings can depend on whether the dispute concerns immigration, presidential removal authority, federal spending, or the scope of emergency relief. And whereas some justices have supported federal executive positions at broadly similar rates across presidencies, others appear far more likely to do so depending on whether the president is a Republican or Democrat.…
items.t: Which justices favor the Trump administration the most (and least) on the emergency docket?

items.title: What do these Supreme Court plaintiffs have in common?
items.summary:
Last term in Little v. Hecox , which concerned whether states could bar transgender female athletes from participating in girl’s and women’s sports, Justice Sonia Sotomayor asked Idaho Solicitor General Alan Hurst: “Do you dispute that having a case named after you makes your infamy ... live forever? ... You don't think that Brown and any of the other named plaintiffs that we have in famous cases dr[ew] … attention to those people as people?” Sotomayor asked the question in the context of Hecox requesting that the Supreme Court dismiss the case, citing, in part, “negative public scrutiny ... because of this litigation.”

On Tuesdays for the past few months, we have dedicated the “Closer Look” section of SCOTUSblog’s daily newsletter to covering the story of some of the most famous plaintiffs behind landmark Supreme Court cases.

Now 16 installments in, we thought it would be a good time to take a step back and assess what’s been learned. In this article, we offer a glimpse at the lives of a baker, a farmer, an executive director at Planned Parenthood, two students, and a leader of the Ku Klux Klan. But besides having interesting (and sometimes disturbing) life stories, what do they all have in common? Joseph Lochner : Lochner v. New York

items.title: Why the genocide verdict against Myanmar has big implications for Israel | Geoffrey Robertson
items.summary:
Proving the ‘crime of crimes’ against an individual is notoriously difficult, but the ICJ has set a precedent for states to be found liable. Israel could be next

For the first time ever, a state has been found guilty of genocide – that “crime of crimes” – and has been ordered to compensate victims and to prosecute and punish the perpetrators. This judgment came from the international court of justice (ICJ), which has convicted Myanmar of killing and expelling many thousands of Rohingyas in Rakhine state in 2017.

The court did not change the definition of the crime, settled by the genocide convention in 1948 as requiring proof of an intention to destroy, in whole or part, a racial or religious group as such. But it made the prospect of proving this against a nation a good deal easier than against an individual. It set a precedent for its next case concerning state liability, namely the case brought by South Africa against Israel.

Geoffrey Robertson KC was a UN appeal judge and is author of World of War Crimes – Eyeless in Gaza and Beyond

On November 10, The New York Times published an article suggesting that a major piece of the Supreme Court’s Second Amendment jurisprudence is premised on a misquote by the late Justice Antonin Scalia in his 2008 majority opinion in D.C v. Heller , in which the court held that there was an individual right to possess firearms. The essence of the piece is that Scalia used the phrase “dangerous and unusual” to describe those weapons not protected by the right to keep and bear arms, attributing this terminology primarily (or perhaps solely) to the 18th century British jurist William Blackstone. Yet Blackstone’s writings instead use the phrase “dangerous or unusual.”

According to the Times piece, “[t]he consequences of Justice Scalia’s use of ‘and’ rather than ‘or’ have been profound”: “Since all guns are dangerous, courts have had to focus instead on determining whether a type of firearm is unusual, often parsing marketing data and consumer surveys to gauge a weapon’s popularity.” Presumably, if Scalia had used the phrase “dangerous or unusual,” it would be easier for legislatures to ban even certain commonly owned firearms because dangerousness alone would be sufficient to bring a category of weapons outside the amendment’s protective sphere.

The Times story has reverberated quickly, with strong backlash from conservative lawyers and scholars. Such disagreements have focused largely on the specific citation Scalia used.…
items.t: The Second Amendment and an "unusually dangerous" approach to dicta

items.title: Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson and the arc of the law
items.summary:
In September, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson received an award named after the late Justice William Brennan, a liberal lion. In her acceptance speech, Jackson discussed Brennan’s role as the Supreme Court became more conservative, noting that he “believed that even his dissents could make a difference and remind the nation that the pursuit of equal justice under law is an ongoing effort.” Jackson indicated that she agreed with that idea, telling the audience that she saw “dissent[s] as more than just a disagreement with the outcome of a case, I see them as an expression of faith in the future and a demonstration of hope.” As she put it, “However desolate the moment feels, we who write for a future age have hope that the noble and collective work of bending the long arc of the law toward justice will continue.”

Since joining the court in the summer of 2022, Jackson has sought to promote her understanding of that view. Although she has been consistently part of the court’s liberal bloc, even among the three Democratic appointees she has forged a unique role. As her invocation of Brennan suggests, it often appears that her goal is not simply to express disagreement with the majority, but to offer an alternative vision and to speak to the public directly – even if she does so without the support of her fellow liberals.
items.t: Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson and the arc of the law

items.title: The Supreme Court and profanity
items.summary:
Around 2 p.m. on October 30, 1973, John Douglas was driving with his 15-year-old son when he heard a litany of profanity come over the radio. New York’s WBAI, a nonprofit radio station, was airing a program on modern attitudes toward language. Near the end, the station played George Carlin’s “ Filthy Words ” routine, which begins with the comedian saying he’d been thinking about “the words you couldn’t say on the public airwaves; the ones you definitely wouldn’t say, ever.” He went on to repeat those words several times, contrasting them with words like “bastards,” “hell,” and “damn,” which were mostly acceptable, and showing how even some of his list of seven were perfectly fine in other contexts. His point was to show the absurdity of profanity.

The station later said it had chosen Carlin’s routine because it was an “incisive satirical view of the subject under discussion,” in the style of other great satirists like Mark Twain or Mort Sahl. Carlin, the station explained, was doing more than “mouthing obscenities.” He was “using words to satirize as harmless and essentially silly our attitudes towards those words.” 

Before playing the routine, the host had warned that it included language some listeners might find offensive and suggested they return in 15 minutes if they were inclined toward offense. But about a month later, John Douglas complained to the Federal Communications Commission about the transmission which he said was “garbage” and had been broadcast in the presence of his “young son.” He was the only listener to do so. items.title: Justice Sotomayor addresses Supreme Court term limits
items.summary:
As you prepare for a December argument session containing several significant cases, remember to check out (or revisit) the forecasting contest we’re hosting this term in collaboration with Good Judgment Inc . This enables SCOTUS obsessives (and non-obsessives) to forecast how the court will decide the most important cases of the term, and to test that collective judgment against AI models.

At the Court The Supreme Court Building will be closed for Thanksgiving on Thursday and Friday.

The December argument session will begin on Monday, November 30. On Wednesday, December 2, the court will hear argument in Viramontes v. Cook County , on the constitutionality of bans on AR-15s and similar semiautomatic rifles, at 10:00 a.m. EST. We will be live blogging that morning beginning at 9:30 a.m.
